mcqs.question: Why can Kubernetes run containers without Docker installed at all?
options: Kubernetes has its own separate container format unrelated to OCI
This isn't actually possible — Docker is required
Kubernetes only supports a special Docker-free version of containers
Kubernetes talks directly to an OCI-compliant runtime like containerd, which Docker itself also relies on
mcqs.explanation: Docker isn't the foundational layer — it's a CLI and daemon that itself delegates to containerd and runc. Kubernetes can talk to containerd (or another OCI runtime) directly, bypassing Docker entirely, since the OCI spec is what actually standardizes image and runtime behavior.

mcqs.question: A container needs maximum network performance and is trusted to run with no network isolation from the host. Which networking mode fits?
options: host, which shares the host's network namespace directly with no NAT
none, to avoid any network overhead
bridge, since it's the safe default
Container-to-container mode, which is fastest by design
mcqs.explanation: Host networking removes the NAT and virtual interface overhead of bridge mode by sharing the host's network namespace directly — at the cost of network isolation, which is why it's reserved for trusted, performance-critical cases.

mcqs.question: You want live-reloading of source code from a specific folder on your laptop into a dev container. Which storage option is the natural fit?
options: A named volume, since Docker manages it automatically
A bind mount, pointing directly at that host folder
tmpfs, since it's the fastest option
None of these support live file changes
mcqs.explanation: A bind mount maps a specific, known host path directly into the container, which is exactly what live-reload dev setups need. A named volume is Docker-managed storage without a fixed host-visible path, and tmpfs holds data only in memory with no relation to a host folder.
